intro: You have spent years learning what science has found: how cells divide, why the seasons turn, what holds an atom together. This last unit is about something different: how anyone knows any of it, and how you can tell when a claim deserves belief. A doctor in 1854 drew dots on a map and found the cause of cholera before anyone had seen the germ. A scientist in a cornfield saw genes move when the textbooks said they could not. A tiny study of twelve children started a fear that studies of a million children could not confirm. In each case the difference between truth and error was not who was more confident, but who had the better evidence and the more careful reasoning.

The first chapter is about reading evidence: telling correlation from cause, spotting a biased sample, reading a graph whose axis has been trimmed, knowing what a plus-or-minus means, understanding why one paper is a lead and a replicated result is knowledge. It ends with three cases, smoking and cancer, the ozone layer, and vaccines and autism, where careful evidence settled questions that arguments alone never could. The second chapter is about making evidence: asking a question sharp enough to test, designing a fair comparison, collecting data you could defend, building and testing a model or a prototype, and writing and standing behind a claim.

By the end you will plan and carry out an investigation of your own, from a testable question to a public defense. The tools you will use are the same ones that John Snow and Barbara McClintock used, and the same ones that a citizen needs to judge a headline, a product label or a proposal at a city council meeting. Science is not a pile of facts. It is a set of habits for finding out what is true and admitting when you were wrong, and those habits are what this unit is for.
bigQuestion: What makes a claim worth believing, and how do you build one that others should believe?

timeline.t: Francis Bacon argues that knowledge should be built up from careful observation rather than from authority
The Royal Society of London is founded; its motto, Nullius in verba, means take nobody's word for it
James Lind tests six remedies for scurvy on twelve sailors kept under the same conditions
John Snow maps cholera deaths around the Broad Street pump and argues the disease travels in water
Ronald Fisher publishes The Design of Experiments, laying out randomization and control
A British trial of streptomycin for tuberculosis assigns patients to groups at random
Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill report that lung cancer patients are almost all smokers
Barbara McClintock presents evidence that genes can move within a chromosome; few believe her
The United States Surgeon General's committee concludes that smoking causes lung cancer
Mario Molina and Sherwood Rowland predict that CFCs will destroy ozone high in the atmosphere
British Antarctic Survey scientists report the ozone hole; nations sign the Montreal Protocol two years later
The Lancet retracts the 1998 paper linking vaccines and autism after its data are shown to be false

words.d: a statement that answers a scientific question about what happens or why
observations, measurements and data that can be checked and that bear on a claim
a pattern in which two quantities tend to rise or fall together, which does not by itself show cause
a hidden factor that affects both quantities and creates a misleading correlation
a comparison group treated the same as the test group except for the one factor being studied
a systematic difference between a sample and the population it is meant to represent
the range within which the true value of a measurement probably lies
repeating a study independently to see whether the same result appears
the factor an experimenter changes on purpose
the outcome an experimenter measures to see the effect of the change
a simplified representation of a system used to explain and predict, reliable only where its assumptions hold
the measurable requirements a successful engineering design must meet

test.q: John Snow's map showed deaths clustered around one pump. What turned that pattern into a strong argument?
choices: The map was drawn in color
Snow was a well-known doctor
The exceptions, such as the brewery and the workhouse, fit the water explanation and not the bad-air one
The pump handle was removed the same day
test.why: A cluster could have many causes; cases that the rival theory could not explain but the water theory could are what made the case.

test.q: Counties with more churches also have more crime. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Churches cause crime
Crime causes churches to be built
It is impossible to say anything
Larger populations produce both more churches and more crime
test.why: Population size is a confounding variable that drives both counts, creating a correlation without causation.

test.q: Which sample is most likely to represent the opinions of a whole city?
choices: One thousand residents chosen at random from all households
Everyone who calls in to a radio show
Two million car owners who return a mailed survey
The first hundred people who reply online
test.why: Random selection avoids the systematic bias built into volunteer or car-owner samples, regardless of their size.

test.q: A bar chart's vertical axis runs from 9.8 to 10.2 hours, and the bars show 10.1 and 9.9 hours. How does this affect a viewer?
choices: It shows the difference accurately
It makes a 2 percent difference look enormous
It hides the difference completely
It has no effect on perception
test.why: A truncated axis stretches a tiny range across the full height, exaggerating a small difference.

test.q: A scale reads 3 grams with nothing on it. Repeating a measurement ten times and averaging will do what?
choices: Remove the 3-gram error
Halve the 3-gram error
Leave the 3-gram error unchanged, because it is systematic
Turn it into random error
test.why: Averaging reduces random scatter but cannot remove a consistent offset; only calibration catches systematic error.

test.q: A student's calculator shows a density of 0.944700461 g per cubic centimeter from measurements with two significant figures. How should it be reported?
test.why: A result cannot be more precise than its least precise measurement, so two significant figures is the honest report.

test.q: What was decisive in rejecting the 1989 cold fusion claim?
choices: Independent labs could not replicate it
The authors were not chemists
It was announced at a press conference
It was published in the wrong journal
test.why: Replication is the real test; the claim failed it worldwide within months.

test.q: A headline says a food raises the relative risk of a disease by 20 percent. The absolute risk was 5 percent. What is the new absolute risk?
choices: 25 percent
About 6 percent
20 percent
About 1 percent
test.why: Twenty percent of 5 percent is 1 percentage point, so the risk rises from about 5 to about 6 percent.

test.q: How did scientists establish that smoking causes lung cancer without an experiment on people?
choices: They ran a randomized trial on volunteers
They relied on one large survey
They combined strength, dose-response, timing, consistency across studies and a mechanism from animal tests
They waited for the tobacco companies to admit it
test.why: The Bradford Hill questions, answered by many kinds of evidence together, built a causal case that chance could not match.

test.q: Why do the ozone and vaccine cases both count as science working well?
choices: Both first claims were confirmed
Both first claims were rejected
Both were settled by a single famous scientist
In each, independent measurements or large studies decided the question rather than the original claim
test.why: One prediction was confirmed and one was refuted, but in both the weight of independent evidence settled the matter.

test.q: Which of these is a testable question?
choices: Does the salt concentration of water change the temperature at which it freezes, for concentrations from 0 to 10 percent?
Is salt good?
Why is water interesting?
Should people use less salt?
test.why: It names the variable changed, the outcome measured and the range tested; the others have no measurable terms or are questions of value.

test.q: A student tests fertilizer on tomatoes but gives the fertilized plants a sunnier spot. What kind of error is this?
choices: A rounding error
An uncontrolled variable that differs between groups
A problem with the dependent variable
A calibration error
test.why: Sunlight now differs along with fertilizer, so any difference in yield cannot be attributed to fertilizer alone.

test.q: A pendulum model ignores air resistance and works well for small swings but fails for very wide ones. What does this show?
choices: The model is useless
Air resistance does not exist
A model is reliable only where its assumptions hold
Pendulums cannot be modeled
test.why: Every model simplifies; its usefulness is bounded by the range where its assumptions are close enough to true.

test.q: A craft-stick bridge must span 40 centimeters and hold 5 kilograms within a materials budget. Which is a constraint?
choices: It should look attractive
It should hold as much as possible
It should be easy to carry
It must use no more than the materials budget
test.why: A constraint is a firm limit any design must stay within; the others are criteria for judging how good a design is.

test.q: Why should a capstone plan state, before data collection, what result would count against the hypothesis?
choices: So the analysis cannot be quietly changed later to fit the result
Because hypotheses are usually wrong
To make the report longer
Because the timeline requires it
test.why: Deciding in advance what would falsify the claim protects against fooling yourself, the easiest person to fool.

write.prompt: Choose one of the unit's three cases: smoking and lung cancer, the ozone layer, or vaccines and autism. Write a claim about what the evidence shows, support it with at least three specific pieces of evidence from the unit, explain the reasoning that links them, and describe the strongest objection someone could raise and how the evidence answers it.
tips: Claim: one sentence stating what the evidence shows, kept inside what the studies actually tested.
Evidence: use specific studies, numbers and dates from the chapter, such as sample sizes, dose-response patterns or measurements that confirmed a prediction.
Reasoning: explain why each piece of evidence supports the claim, using ideas like control groups, replication, mechanism or the Bradford Hill questions.
The other side: state the best counterclaim honestly, including who made it and why it seemed plausible, then show which evidence answers it.
Uncertainty: say what remained unknown at the time and what later evidence added.
